lesson.title: Esta Es Mi Familia: A Family Photo Share
lesson.subject: spanish

contentBlocks.text: Sol taped up a picture of Sol's family — a mamá sun, a papá sun, and a tiny bebé sun! Today you get to look at a photo of your own family and point to each person.

Look closely at your family photo. Point to [[la abuela]] — that means grandma. Point to [[el abuelo]] — that means grandpa. Some children see their abuela and abuelo every day. Some live far away. Some children live with their abuelos. Say it out loud: 'la abuela,' 'el abuelo.'

Now point to every person in your photo and name them in Spanish: la mamá, el papá, el hermano, la hermana, el bebé, la abuela, el abuelo. Maybe your photo has one of each. Maybe it has two mamás, or one papá, or three hermanos, or a dog you love! Every family is different, and every one is a familia.
You pointed to your whole familia and named each person in Spanish — even la abuela and el abuelo! Tomorrow, Sol tells a story about a big family day full of hugs.

config.instructions: Match the Spanish family word to the person.

objectives: Add la abuela (grandma) and el abuelo (grandpa) to the family words from Day 1
Point to and name each member of their own family in Spanish while looking at a photo
materialsNeeded: A family photo, or a few photos, that your child can point to
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Sit with Sol and your child's family photo.
2. Teach the two new words: point to a grandparent in the photo (or hold up a picture) and say la abuela for grandma, el abuelo for grandpa — have your child echo each.
3. Say warmly that families are different: some children live with their abuelos, some see them on video calls, some far away — all of it is normal.
4. Now walk the photo together. Point to each person and have your child name them in Spanish — la mamá, el papá, el hermano, la hermana, el bebé, la abuela, el abuelo — helping with any word.
5. If your child's family does not match the word list one-to-one (two mamás, one parent, a guardian, many siblings, a beloved pet), name who IS there and skip who is not — the point is naming your own real family.
6. Play the on-screen matching game together, reading each word aloud since your child may not read yet.
7. Close by asking: 'What is la abuela in English? Point to el bebé in the photo.'
differentiationTips: Struggling: name each person for your child first and have them just repeat and point
Ready for more: your child says a short sentence for each person — 'Esta es mi mamá,' 'Este es mi abuelo'
There is no 'right' family in the photo — a child naming a tío, a madrina, or a foster hermano is doing exactly the task
teacherGuide.answerKey: This is a spoken pointing-and-naming activity — success looks like your child adding la abuela and el abuelo and naming the real people in their own photo. In the matching game: la mamá → mom, el papá → dad, el hermano → brother, la hermana → sister, la abuela → grandma, el abuelo → grandpa, el bebé → baby, la familia → the whole family.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Builds week 7's WA-WL-2015.2.1 Cultures target by tying the Spanish family words to the child's own family and naming out loud that families take many shapes. Matches the scope-and-sequence's Day 2 design (a family photo share — children point and name mamá, papá, hermanos), extends it with the grandparent words the Day 3 story needs, and gives the full set a quiet on-screen rep through the matching activity.
